steps.title: When a situation is binomial
steps.body:
A count \(X\) is binomial, \(X \sim \mathrm{B}(n,\,p)\), when four things hold:
•  a fixed number of trials, \(n\)
•  each trial is a success or a failure
•  the probability of success, \(p\), is the same every time
•  the trials are independent

Twelve free throws, each scored with probability \(0.7\), independently: \(X \sim \mathrm{B}(12,\,0.7)\).
Write this line first in every binomial question; it earns the method mark.
steps.code:
\(X \sim \mathrm{B}(n,\,p)\), \(X\) = number of successes in \(n\) trials
\(\mathrm{P}(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\)   (formula booklet; the calculator does this)

steps.title: Which of these counts is binomial?
opts: The number of sixes in \(10\) rolls of a fair die
The number of aces in \(5\) cards dealt from a pack without replacement
The number of rolls until the first six
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Fixed \(n=10\), success or not, constant \(p=\frac16\), independent rolls: \(\mathrm{B}(10,\,\frac16)\).
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. Cards without replacement change \(p\) each time, and “rolls until the first six” has no fixed \(n\). The sixes in \(10\) rolls are binomial: \(\mathrm{B}(10,\,\frac16)\).

fig.caption: P(X ≤ 8): the Cdf adds the bars from 0 up to and including 8.

nspire.body:
\(\mathrm{P}(X\le8)\) is the sum of the bars for \(0,1,\ldots,8\). The Cdf does that sum in one call. On the Nspire, Binomial Cdf takes a Lower and an Upper bound, so \(\mathrm{P}(X\le8)\) is Lower 0, Upper 8.

The words decide which bars are in. “At most \(8\)”, “no more than \(8\)” and “\(8\) or fewer” all allow a score of exactly \(8\), so the bar at \(8\) is in: \(X\le8\), Upper \(8\).

“Fewer than \(8\)” does not allow \(8\): that is \(X<8\). The calculator has no “less than” option, its upper bound is always included, so convert it yourself. \(X\) only takes whole numbers, so “less than \(8\)” is the same as “\(7\) or fewer”: \(\mathrm{P}(X<8)=\mathrm{P}(X\le7)\), Upper \(7\). Typing \(8\) here adds one bar too many, the most common binomial slip in exams.

The Cdf counts from \(0\) upwards, so “at least” needs the complement. Be careful which bar is the last one removed:
•  “at least \(9\)” keeps the bar at \(9\): \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge9)=1-\mathrm{P}(X\le8)\), not \(1-\mathrm{P}(X\le9)\)

fig.caption: P(7 ≤ X ≤ 10): bars 7 to 10. From Cdf values: P(X ≤ 10) − P(X ≤ 6).

•  remove everything up to \(6\): \(\mathrm{P}(X\le6)\)
•  the bar at \(7\) must stay, so subtract \(\mathrm{P}(X\le6)\), not \(\mathrm{P}(X\le7)\)

steps.title: Mean and variance
steps.body:
For \(X \sim \mathrm{B}(n,\,p)\), both in the formula booklet:
•  mean: \(\mathrm{E}(X)=np\)
•  variance: \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\)

For the free throws, \(\mathrm{E}(X)=12\times0.7=8.4\): over many sets of \(12\), the player scores \(8.4\) on average.

If a question gives the mean and variance and asks for \(n\) and \(p\), divide one by the other: \(\dfrac{np(1-p)}{np}=1-p\).

parts: ✗ \(np\) is the mean; the square root is the standard deviation. \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\).

steps.title: Least \(n\): “at least one”
steps.body:
“How many trials are needed so that the probability of at least one success is more than \(0.99\)?”
•  complement: \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge1)=1-\mathrm{P}(X=0)=1-(1-p)^n\)
•  condition: \(1-(1-p)^n>0.99\), i.e. \((1-p)^n<0.01\)
•  solve: a table of values of \(n\), or logarithms; give the smallest whole number that works

Show the values either side of the boundary; that is the method mark.

sets.label: \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge1)=\)
steps: Two distributions. The normal gives the probability for one bag; the binomial counts bags.
\(p=\mathrm{P}(M<480)\) with \(\mu=500\), \(\sigma=12\): Normal Cdf gives \(0.04779\). Keep the full value.
\(1-0.6128=0.387\). Check: about \(5\%\) per bag, ten bags: a bit under \(50\%\), since the chances overlap.
wrongs: That is \(p\) for one bag. Now the binomial over \(10\) bags.

\(0.478\) is \(10p\): probabilities do not add like that.

steps: “At least two” has no single-formula complement: \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge2)=1-\mathrm{P}(X\le1)\), and \(\mathrm{P}(X\le1)\) depends on \(n\) through the Cdf.
Try values of \(n\) in Binomial Cdf (\(0\) to \(1\)) until \(1-\mathrm{P}(X\le1)\) first reaches \(0.9\). A table of \(1-\mathrm{binomCdf}(n,\,0.2,\,0,\,1)\) against \(n\) is fastest.

wrongs: \(11\) is the answer for “at least one”. Here it is at least two.

questions.stem: A factory produces light bulbs. It is known that \(5\%\) of the bulbs are defective. A random sample of \(20\) bulbs is taken, and \(X\) is the number of defective bulbs in the sample.

parts.label: (a)
parts.figCap: X ~ B(20, 0.05): the bar at k = 2 (bars beyond 6 are too small to see).
wrongs: \(0.925\) is \(\mathrm{P}(X\le2)\), the cdf. “\(X=2\)” is one bar: pdf.
That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=1)\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the probability that at most \(2\) bulbs are defective.
parts.figCap: At most 2: the bars 0, 1 and 2 added (cdf up to 2).
wrongs: \(0.736\) is \(\mathrm{P}(X\le1)\): “at most \(2\)” includes the bar at \(2\).
That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=2)\) alone.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one bulb is defective.
parts.figCap: Everything except the bar at 0: the complement.
wrongs: That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=0)\); subtract it from \(1\).
\(0.264\) is \(1-\mathrm{P}(X\le1)=\mathrm{P}(X\ge2)\): the bar at \(1\) was removed too.

questions.stem: Seeds of a certain plant germinate with probability \(0.8\), independently of each other. A tray contains \(10\) seeds, and \(X\) is the number that germinate.

parts.label: (a)
parts.figCap: X ~ B(10, 0.8) peaks at the mean, np = 8.
wrongs: \(1.26\) is the standard deviation \(\sqrt{1.6}\); the variance is \(1.6\).
\(2\) is \(n(1-p)\), the expected number that do not germinate.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the probability that at least \(8\) seeds in a tray germinate.
parts.figCap: At least 8: the bars 8, 9, 10, which is 1 − P(X ≤ 7).
wrongs: \(0.376\) is \(1-\mathrm{P}(X\le8)=\mathrm{P}(X\ge9)\): the bar at \(8\) was removed. Subtract \(\mathrm{P}(X\le7)\).
\(0.322\) is \(\mathrm{P}(X\le7)\): forgot the “\(1-\)”.
That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=8)\) alone.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Five trays are planted. Find the probability that exactly \(3\) of the \(5\) trays have at least \(8\) seeds germinating.
parts.figCap: A second binomial: the number of trays, Y ~ B(5, 0.678), with p from part (b).
parts.note: The structure, a binomial whose \(p\) is the answer to an earlier part, appears in almost every session. Follow-through applies to your (b).
wrongs: That is the probability for one tray; the question is about \(3\) of \(5\) trays.
\(0.259\) is \(\binom53\) left out, or \(p\) rounded to \(0.68\); keep the full value.
That is \(\mathrm{P}(Y=4)\).

questions.stem: An archer hits the target with probability \(0.3\) on each shot, independently.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the least number of shots the archer must take so that the probability of hitting the target at least once is greater than \(0.95\).

notes: P(at least one hit) = 1 − 0.7ⁿ, against n

parts.figCap: Bars show 1 − 0.7ⁿ for n = 3 to 12: the first to pass 0.95 is n = 9.
parts.note: Show the values either side of the boundary. A table of \(0.7^{n}\) on the GDC is the quickest way.
wrongs: \(n=8\) gives \(1-0.7^{8}=0.942\), not above \(0.95\). One more shot.
\(10\) works but is not the least: \(9\) already gives \(0.960\).
That is the probability at \(n=9\); the question asks for \(n\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The archer takes \(10\) shots. Find the probability that exactly \(3\) shots hit the target.
wrongs: \(0.650\) is \(\mathrm{P}(X\le3)\): cdf, not pdf.
That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=2)\).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Given that the archer hits the target at least once in the \(10\) shots, find the probability that exactly \(3\) shots hit the target.
parts.figCap: Condition X ≥ 1 removes the bar at 0 from the denominator; the event X = 3 lies inside it.
wrongs: That is \(\mathrm{P}(X=3)\) alone; divide by \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge1)\).
\(0.259\) multiplied by \(\mathrm{P}(X\ge1)\); a condition divides.
That is the denominator.
